Offboard Artificial Intelligence Guides Low Cost Drone for Oil Palm Pollination

Agricultural engineers have developed an autonomous pollination support system that couples a compact unmanned aerial vehicle with an external artificial intelligence computing terminal, achieving an 88.23 percent normal fruit set during field evaluations in an oil palm plantation. Published in Smart Agricultural Technology, the investigation addresses a longstanding operational bottleneck in tropical agriculture, where commercial yields of oil palm heavily depend on the efficacy of pollination across extensive cultivation acreage. Conventional operations rely on natural insect pollinators such as the weevil Elaeidobius kamerunicus alongside extensive manual pollination crews. However, these traditional approaches remain vulnerable to adverse environmental conditions, fluctuations in insect populations, shortages in field labor, and inconsistent mechanical pollen application across vast and challenging agricultural terrains. By moving computationally demanding computer vision and mission decision algorithms off the aerial vehicle and housing them within an intelligent ground controller, the engineering team demonstrated that a lightweight 3.5-inch aerial platform can execute complex agricultural flight workflows without carrying expensive or power-hungry onboard computing units.

Autonomous flight underneath dense agricultural canopies introduces severe robotic challenges that standard aerial mapping and broadcast spraying systems rarely confront. In mature oil palm plantations, tree crowns form overlapping vegetative canopies that severely degrade global navigation satellite system reception through physical signal attenuation and multipath distortions, preventing reliance on global positioning coordinates for close-proximity navigation. Furthermore, commercial groves feature visually repetitive geometric patterns of tree trunks measuring between 1 and 5 meters in height and up to 152 centimeters in circumference, interspersed with drooping fronds that present immediate collision hazards. Standard positioning techniques cannot provide the sub-meter precision required to maneuver within reach of reproductive plant structures. To overcome these constraints, the researchers structured their robotic operational framework into seven distinct sequential stages: aerial tree geo-tagging, satellite-guided waypoint approach, vision-based obstacle avoidance, transitional switching from global navigation to visual servoing, close-range trunk-guided approach, circumferential orbiting inspection, and targeted pollen discharge.

To bypass the weight, heat, and power penalties associated with mounting advanced graphics processing hardware directly on the airframe, the platform utilizes an asymmetric computational partition. High-level image inference, coordinate transformations, mission logic, and navigation control operate within Robot Operating System 2 on a ground-based NVIDIA Jetson Nano P3450 embedded into an intelligent remote controller. The physical drone consists of a compact SpeedyBee 3.5-inch carbon frame equipped with four SB-2006 1950KV brushless motors, a Mateksys H743V4 flight controller running ArduPilot firmware, an MTF-01 optical-flow sensor for low-altitude stabilization, and a 6S 2100 milliampere-hour battery delivering approximately 15 minutes of operational endurance. High-definition digital video and flight telemetry generated by the aircraft are broadcast via a Walksnail Avatar first-person-view digital link. On the ground station, vision algorithms process incoming video frames, while an Arduino Nano microcontroller translates generated velocity commands into pulse-position modulation signals injected into a Radiomaster Pocket ExpressLRS radio transmitter. This architecture ensures that should a collision occur during canopy maneuvering, the costly computing hardware remains safe with the operator on the ground.

The system relies on a dual-scale visual perception strategy that alternates operational references according to flight altitude and operational scale. For plantation-level mapping, an aerial camera view captures tree canopies, which are processed by a single-class YOLOv11n convolutional neural network trained on 6,980 images to locate palm crowns. Once the drone descends into the sub-canopy environment, a second YOLOv11n network trained on 1,362 frontal images takes over, detecting tree trunks to guide fine-scale proximity maneuvering. Trunks provide an exceptionally reliable visual landmark because their rigid vertical structures remain unaffected by wind turbulence or seasonal foliage changes. When evaluated on independent test datasets, the frontal trunk detector achieved a precision of 0.861, a recall of 0.828, and a mean average precision at an intersection-over-union threshold of 0.50 of 0.925. The aerial crown detector registered a precision of 0.831, a recall of 0.677, and an intersection-over-union mean average precision of 0.698, a performance level sufficient for coarse target selection despite background canopy clutter.

Accurate tree geo-tagging requires integrating continuous telemetry directly from the video stream without adding excessive computational overhead to the ground station. Rather than deploying a heavy secondary neural network for optical character recognition, the researchers implemented a normalized cross-correlation template matching routine that monitors a fixed region of the on-screen display showing coordinates, altitude, and heading. This template matching technique achieved 100 percent character recognition accuracy while requiring an average processing latency of just 0.000416 seconds per frame, outperforming convolutional character recognizers that recorded 90.373 percent accuracy at 0.037564 seconds. Detected crown centers in normalized camera coordinates are subsequently transformed into local metric frames using calibrated intrinsic parameters, including an effective focal length of approximately 4.46 millimeters, alongside drone altitude and attitude matrices. To prevent duplicate entries when trees temporarily pass out of view, the system couples DeepSORT temporal tracking with spatial threshold reassociation, storing localized palms in a persistent database with unique global identifiers that track operational status from unvisited to visited.

During field localization experiments over an 868.21 square meter plantation plot traversed in 34 seconds at speeds up to 5.82 meters per second, the aerial mapping routine located candidate trees with a mean geolocation error of 3.551 meters. While this variance exceeds the tolerance required for direct physical pollen delivery, it provides an adequate coarse guidance coordinate for satellite-based transit. The navigation state machine selects the nearest unvisited target tree and executes global navigation waypoint guidance until the platform closes to within a four-meter transition threshold. Once within four meters of the target coordinate, the system automatically transitions from global satellite navigation to local visual servoing. Across eight dedicated flight trials testing this handoff under dense canopy conditions, the transition achieved a 100 percent success rate, seamlessly transferring flight control from satellite guidance to frontal trunk tracking.

Close-range maneuvering relies on continuous visual feedback, but raw neural network bounding boxes frequently suffer from jitter caused by aerodynamic buffeting, vibration, and shifting shadows. To stabilize tracking, the control layer channels horizontal image coordinates and bounding box widths through a constant-velocity Kalman filter before computing control inputs. In quantitative benchmarks evaluating 2,038 video frames, raw YOLO detections yielded 1,702 stable frames and 336 unstable frames, reflecting an 83.51 percent tracking stability rate.
